China is now the world's second-largest economy and its most populous country, with a booming consumer market and an ambitious development strategy. But it also has a large and increasingly assertive military, a growing economic presence across Asia, Africa and Latin America, and a longstanding territorial dispute with Russia over the border regions of the Far East.

Putin has tried to navigate this complex relationship by maintaining a degree of strategic ambiguity. At times, he has signaled a desire to ally with China against Western powers, while at other times, Moscow has sought closer ties with the U.S. to counterbalance China.

But Putin's attempts to cultivate close relations with China have been complicated by the two countries' shared border with the war-torn Central Asian republic of Tajikistan. Russia has stationed thousands of troops in Tajikistan as part of its anti-terrorism efforts, but China has shown increasing interest in the region as well.

Indeed, China is pouring billions of dollars of aid and investment into Central Asia as part of its Belt and Road initiative, a massive development project that aims to build a network of roads and railways link China to Europe via Central Asia.

China's growing influence in the region has alarmed Russia, which views the area as its own backyard. In response to Beijing's growing assertiveness, Putin has recently been seeking to strengthen ties with Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, two other Central Asian republics with large Muslim populations and borders with China.

The question is, will China's growing influence in Central Asia prompt Russia to become more aggressive in the region? Or will it lead to a more collaborative relationship between the two countries?

A few years ago, when Alex was in fifth grade, he started asking his mother questions: Why did his birth parents abandon him? Why did they give birth to him in secret? Why didn't they come to find him?

Knowing the answers to those questions would help him better understand himself, he thought, and he hoped that it would help fill the void he felt in his life. He was 11, after all, and was growing more curious about the world. But Kimberly wasn't ready to share the story of her son's birth with her children. So she told him to be patient, that the time would come when he would learn everything he needed to know.

Lo-fi is not just music, it is a lifestyle. It's a way to appreciate simplicity and imperfection, to find beauty in the rough edges and to enjoy the process of creating rather than the end product itself, much like the concept of Wabi-Sabi in Japanese culture.
